Provenance Inventory

Source: PROVENANCE.md

Package: edaphos 0.9.0 — Digital Soil Mapping with Causal, Physics-Informed and Generative Methods Commit: 8f23ddf Compiled: 2026-08-28

This document answers a specific question: does edaphos distribute soil data it has no right to distribute? In particular, does it contain the datasets datsoilspc or svrc_example, or material from the USDA — the Kellogg Soil Survey Laboratory (KSSL), the National Cooperative Soil Survey (NCSS), RaCA, SSURGO or STATSGO?

Every number below is measured from the repository rather than asserted, and §7 gives the commands to re-derive each one. The machine-readable form is tools/provenance-inventory.json, regenerated by tools/provenance-inventory.R in about two seconds.

1. The two named datasets

datsoilspc and svrc_example do not exist in this repository and never have. The search covered:

Surface searched Result
Working tree — R/, man/, tests/, vignettes/, data-raw/, inst/, DESCRIPTION, NAMESPACE, README.md, NEWS.md 0 files
Every object name inside all 27 shipped data artefacts, read and walked recursively 0 occurrences
Every blob that has ever existed in the repository — 3,865 unique blobs across 5,265 objects, spanning all 227 commits and all 25 refs, including blobs since rewritten out of every branch 0 occurrences

The history search reads the git object database directly rather than walking revisions, which is both faster and strictly more thorough: it sees content that was committed and later removed from every branch, which a git log walk no longer reaches.

2. USDA, Kellogg / KSSL, NCSS, RaCA, SSURGO, STATSGO

Here the honest answer is more interesting than a flat denial, so it is given in full.

2.1 What is genuinely present

Two of the 1,095 soil profiles behind the Cerrado case study carry the WoSIS dataset identifier US-NCSS. They were obtained through ISRIC’s WoSIS 2019 snapshot, not from any USDA service. WoSIS records their licence, and it is this:

Licence recorded by WoSIS Profiles
Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) 842
Attribution-NonCommercial 4.0 International (CC BY-NC 4.0) 250
CC0 1.0 Universal Public Domain Dedication 1
U.S. Public Domain — usa.gov/publicdomain/label/1.0 2

The two US-NCSS profiles are exactly the two profiles that WoSIS labels U.S. Public Domain. That is the U.S. Government’s own public-domain dedication, which places no restriction on redistribution.

No record-level data from those two profiles is shipped. What the package contains is a five-row aggregate table — one row per contributing dataset, holding a count, a year range and a median:

    dataset_id n_profiles year_min year_max soc_median_gkg
1    BR-Cooper        838     1960     1986           13.8
2   BR-Bernoux        250     1973     1982           11.8
3   BR-RioDoce          4     1982     1982           25.2
4      US-NCSS          2     1967     1980           27.0
5 WD-Mangroves          1     2010     2010           33.2

This is the only occurrence of any of the six USDA-related terms inside any shipped data artefact.

2.2 What is present but is not data

USDA and NRCS appear in exactly two files, R/fixtures.R and the manual page generated from it, and in both cases the sentence is a disclaimer telling users to obtain real data themselves:

edaphos does not bundle or redistribute third-party soil data. Real profiles are the user’s to obtain from the upstream services directly — ISRIC WoSIS, the SoilData Dataverse, USDA-NRCS — under those services’ own licences, which vary per record.

One hyperlink in the published documentation site points to https://ncss-tech.github.io/aqp/reference/sp4.html — the reference page for the sp4 example dataset of the aqp R package, hosted on the NCSS technical team’s GitHub organisation. It is a link to another package’s documentation. No data crosses it.

2.3 What looked present and is not

A naïve byte-level search of the repository reports KSSL once, RaCA once and NCSS in a Word manuscript. All three are coincidence, not content. .rds files are xz-compressed, .docx is a ZIP and .png pixel data is DEFLATE — a four-letter sequence turns up in compressed streams by chance. Decompressing each one first and searching the actual content resolves all three:

Apparent hit Where the bytes are What it actually is
KSSL PNG image data of a DAG plot the byte run ksSL inside an IDAT stream
RaCA xz stream of benchmark_wosis_p4_p5_p7.rds RACA between high-bit bytes; absent after decompression
NCSS DEFLATE stream of paper/plos-manuscript.docx absent from the unzipped XML

Kellogg, SSURGO and STATSGO return zero occurrences on every surface, compressed or not.

3. What the package actually ships

27 data artefacts: 24 .rds bundles in inst/extdata/ and 3 .rda datasets in data/.

The three exported datasets are synthetic. br_cerrado, br_amazon and br_pantanal are each a 45 × 45 pixel grid of simulated covariates with a synthesised SOC response, documented as such and generated by data-raw/prepare_br_cerrado.R. The two fixture_* bundles are likewise synthetic stand-ins.

Thirteen of the 27 bundles carry a strip note. On 2026-08-28, commit 8f23ddf (“fix!: stop shipping third-party soil measurements”) ran data-raw/strip_third_party_records.R, which removed every element carrying a third-party measurement or an upstream identifier while keeping the aggregate tables the published results rest on. The manifest of what was removed is committed at data-raw/build/stripped_elements.csv, which names each removed element and the reason, for example:

  • piml_coverage — $coverage (150 rows): $truth was verbatim upstream laboratory SOC keyed to a real profile identifier
  • pilar8_real_pedons — $cv (5,458 rows): measured SOC at 7 depth nodes for 1,022 real pedons
  • capstone_campaign_results — $wosis_profiles (250), $piml_profile_obs (9): real coordinates and measured SOC
  • piml_prior_sensitivity — $profile_id: a bare upstream identifier with no measurements attached, removed because it still identifies a pedon

The reasoning recorded in that script draws the line this way: a per-fold RMSE is a statement about a method; a 1,095-element vector of measured SOC is the dataset.

One inconsistency in the audit trail, reported rather than tidied away. The committed manifest lists 11 bundles, while the script that wrote it declares 13 — it also strips case_cerrado_results ($profiles, 1,095 × 70, and $emb_cols) and causal_cerrado_real_v2 ($profiles, 3,077 × 11, described in the script as the widest real WoSIS pull in the package). The committed CSV predates those two sections and was not regenerated; the script is not re-runnable once it has run, because its inputs no longer exist.

The discrepancy is in the paperwork, not in the artefacts. Both bundles were checked directly and both have had their payload removed: $profiles and $emb_cols are absent from each, and both carry the strip note. The manifest under-reports what was removed; it does not over-report it.

4. Geographic extent

Every coordinate pair reachable inside every shipped artefact was extracted and tested against a deliberately generous Brazil bounding box and against the United States:

Coordinates shipped 7,392
Falling inside Brazil 7,392
Falling inside the United States 0
Extent longitude −60.50 to −44.00, latitude −22.00 to −2.90

The Brazil box is loose on purpose: the claim under test is “these points are not in the United States”, and a loose box makes that harder to pass, not easier.

Of these, 6,075 belong to the three synthetic grids. The remaining 1,317 were checked individually:

  • 424 in capstone_campaign_results.rds — 416 fall exactly on a regular 10 × 10 lattice spanning −50° to −48° longitude and −16° to −14° latitude at a spacing of exactly 0.222222°. The other 8 sit on a 0.2° lattice and are the observation sites of a data-assimilation demonstration. Real soil profiles do not fall on an exact lattice; these are simulation grids.
  • 893 in the two fixture_* bundles — synthetic by construction and documented as such.

4.1 The stronger test: collision against the real coordinates

A bounding box tests where points are. The check that the accusation actually calls for tests what they are not — whether anything still shipped coincides with the real coordinates that once were here.

The pre-strip state of all 27 bundles is recoverable from commit d8c1998, the parent of the strip. Reading them back and subtracting what survives gives the coordinate universe the strip removed: 3,047 distinct real coordinates, from case_cerrado_results (1,081), causal_cerrado_real_v2 (2,872), causal_cerrado_real (1,081), piml_external_anchors (1,060), piml_wosis_cerrado (1,060), capstone_campaign_results (250), soildata_uberaba_bd (83) and temporal_cerrado_results (10). That set is computed by difference rather than read from the manifest, which is why it is trustworthy where the manifest is not — see §3.

Intersecting everything still shipped against those 3,047 coordinates:

Artefact Points Collisions
br_amazon 2,025 0
br_cerrado 2,025 0
br_pantanal 2,025 0
fixture_wosis_like 833 0
fixture_soildata_like 60 0
capstone_campaign_results 424 1

The three exported datasets are further confirmed as complete regular lattices: 45 × 45 with all 2,025 cells filled and a single constant spacing on each axis (0.009091° for br_amazon and br_pantanal, 0.007955° × 0.006818° for br_cerrado). Real soil profiles do not fill a rectangular lattice.

The single collision, run down. It is the point (−47.9, −14.1), row 8 of capstone_campaign_results$temporal_results$obs_locations, which also appears among the coordinates removed from temporal_cerrado_results. It is not a leaked profile. What was removed from that bundle is itself a perfect 10 × 10 grid at exactly 0.2° spacing spanning −47.9 to −46.1 by −15.9 to −14.1: raster cell centres of a simulation domain, holding gridded NDVI, precipitation and temperature, not soil sampling sites. Both bundles describe the same domain, so they share its grid nodes. The eight rows the package still ships carry two columns, lon and lat, and no measurement of any kind.

4.2 The automated guard

tests/testthat/test-no-third-party-data.R enforces this on every test run. It walks each shipped bundle recursively to depth 12 and descends where a names-based check cannot see: into lm/glm/nls internals — $residuals, $fitted.values, $qr, $effects — and into the enclosing environments of closures. It was written after a bundle that had been “slimmed” by nulling $model turned out to still ship residuals named by real WoSIS profile ids, in three places the author believed were empty. It flags coordinate columns, columns and row names holding upstream-shaped identifiers, and atomic vectors keyed by them. A companion test constructs that exact defect and asserts the scanner fires on it, on the principle that a guard never shown to fail is not a guard.

5. Provenance records

Each bundle records the script that produced it and that script’s hash. Of the 27 artefacts, 16 carry a verifiable script_sha256, and all 16 verify — recomputing the hash from the script on disk reproduces the recorded value.

One caveat for anyone checking by hand: edaphos hashes a script’s lines joined by newline through digest, not the raw file bytes, so shasum -a 256 <file> will legitimately disagree with a recorded script_sha256. The convention is implemented in .script_hash() in R/provenance.R and travels with its own algorithm tag. Comparing the two conventions looks like a tampered file and is not one.

6. Upstream sources, as declared

The Cerrado case study bundle declares its sources in the artefact itself:

Layer Source
Area of interest IBGE Biomes via geobr (Pereira & Gonçalves 2019)
Soil organic carbon WoSIS snapshot 2019 (Batjes et al. 2020), CC-BY-4.0, ISRIC
Soil covariates SoilGrids 250 m (Hengl et al. 2017), CC-BY-4.0, ISRIC
Climate WorldClim 2.1 (Fick & Hijmans 2017)
Elevation SRTM 30-arcsec (Jarvis et al. 2008; NASA public domain)
Land cover ESA WorldCover 2020 v100 (Zanaga et al. 2021), CC-BY-4.0

No USDA service appears among them. The USDA-derived profiles reached the package through WoSIS, which aggregates national contributions and records a licence per record.

7. How to verify this yourself

Every claim above is reproducible from a checkout. None of these commands needs network access.

Regenerate the full inventory, including the §4.1 collision check — it reads the pre-strip bundles back out of git, so it needs no network and no archived copy (~4 seconds):

Rscript tools/provenance-inventory.R

Run the automated guard of §4.2, and the companion test that proves it fires:

Rscript -e 'pkgload::load_all("."); testthat::test_file("tests/testthat/test-no-third-party-data.R")'

Search every blob that has ever existed in the repository:

sh tools/history-term-scan.sh "datsoilspc|svrc_example|KSSL|Kellogg|NCSS|RaCA|SSURGO|STATSGO"

That command prints 1 kssl, 58 ncss and 1 raca, and prints nothing for datsoilspc, svrc_example, Kellogg, SSURGO and STATSGO — a term that never existed produces no line at all. It counts raw bytes, so its three non-zero lines are the coincidences dissected in §2.3 plus the aqp documentation hyperlink of §2.2. The next command is the one that searches content rather than bytes.

Search the decompressed content of every shipped data artefact — this is the search that matters, since raw-byte searches produce the false positives described in §2.3:

for f in inst/extdata/*.rds data/*.rda; do gunzip -c "$f" 2>/dev/null | grep -oa -i -E "KSSL|NCSS|RaCA|SSURGO|STATSGO|Kellogg|USDA|NRCS|datsoilspc|svrc_example" | sort -u | sed "s|^|$f: |"; done

Read the manifest of everything removed in the strip:

cat data-raw/build/stripped_elements.csv

8. What this inventory does not establish

Three limits, stated so that the document is not read for more than it supports.

  1. It covers this repository. It says nothing about any other copy, fork or distribution of the package.

  2. A name search cannot find data hidden under a different name. The coordinate audit in §4 is the stronger evidence, because it tests the content rather than the labels: no point in any shipped artefact lies in the United States, and the non-synthetic coordinates all fall on exact lattices. Anyone wanting a still stronger check should search for a known pedon identifier or a known coordinate pair from the dataset they believe was copied; §7 shows how.

  3. It reports what WoSIS declares. The licence table in §2.1 is WoSIS’s own metadata, carried through unmodified. This document verifies that the package handled those records consistently with that metadata; it does not independently audit ISRIC’s licensing of its upstream contributions.
